extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting claim language during patent examination, including when claim terms receive ordinary meaning, special definitions from the specification, disavowal, the effect of preambles, and the meaning of transitional phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term defined by implication (usage in specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of a particular claim term may be defined by implication, that is, according to the usage of the term in the context of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp., Vitronics. But where the specification is ambiguous as to whether the inventor used claim terms inconsistent with their ordinary meaning, the ordinary meaning will apply (example: Merck v. Teva — 'about' should be given its plain and ordinary meaning 'approximately' rather than 'exactly' when the specification passage is too ambiguous to redefine it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not interpret claims to omit a disclosed embodiment absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be interpreted in a way that would omit a disclosed embodiment, absent evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intrinsic evidence (specification/prosecution history) shows embodiments, claim construction should avoid reading claims so narrowly that those embodiments are excluded unless there is clear contrary evidence. Example: court found specification defined two different types of 'Wide' point of view while claim language was broader; claim required one or the other but not both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disavowal (disclaimer) requires clear and unmistakable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may rebut the presumption of plain meaning by clearly disavowing the full scope of the claim term in the specification; disavowal is only considered when it is clear and unmistakable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See SciMed Life Sys. v. Advanced Cardiovascular Sys.; disavowal can, in some cases, be made by implication (e.g., specification contains only disparaging remarks about a feature and every embodiment excludes that feature — In re Abbott Diabetes Care). Examiner should make any implicit disavowal-based interpretation clear on the record. See also MPEP § 2173.05(a). Note: prosecution history estoppel is inapplicable during prosecution to limit claims of pending applications (see In re Clarke for distinction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowchart for determining meaning of a claim term (non-112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision sequence examiners should follow to ascertain proper claim interpretation based on plain meaning/BRI when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is not invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) Determine whether claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art. If yes, check specification for a special definition. If spec provides a special definition, use it and acknowledge/identify it in the Office action; if not, apply the ordinary meaning. (2) If the term does not have an ordinary meaning, check the specification for a meaning. If no reasonably clear meaning can be ascribed after considering spec and prior art, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). If the specification provides a meaning, the examiner should use the meaning provided and may acknowledge it in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of preamble must be determined case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case; there is no litmus test defining when a preamble limits the scope of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle: '[A] claim preamble has the import that the claim as a whole suggests for it.' Evaluate the preamble in context of entire claim and record; see Catalina Mktg., Bell Communications Research, Pitney Bowes for guideposts and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble statements limiting structure are claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any terminology in the preamble that limits the structure of the claimed invention must be treated as a claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the entirety of the application to understand what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass without importing extraneous limitations from the specification. Cases: Corning Glass Works, Pac-Tec, In re Stencel (example where collar structure in preamble limited the driver claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble reciting purpose or intended use may be non-limiting unless it imparts structural difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If the body of a claim fully and intrinsically sets forth all limitations of the claimed invention, and the preamble merely states the purpose or intended use, the preamble is not considered a limitation; however, if the preamble's stated purpose results in a structural (or manipulative for process claims) difference from the prior art, it may limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the preamble gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim (Pitney Bowes). During examination, determine whether the recited purpose/intent produces a structural difference over prior art; a prior art structure capable of performing the intended use meets the limiting intended-use preamble. Reliance on the preamble during prosecution to distinguish prior art can transform the preamble into a claim limitation (Metabolite Labs., Catalina Marketing). Examples and contrasting cases provided (Rowe v. Dror, Jansen, Poly‑America, Intirtool). See MPEP § 2112-2112.02 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase 'comprising' is open-ended/inclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' (synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by') is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is case-by-case, but 'comprising' signals that named elements are essential while permitting additional elements (Mars Inc., Invitrogen, Genentech, Gillette). Example: a claim 'comprising' a group of blades can encompass devices with additional blades. See MPEP § 2111.03 I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase 'consisting of' is closed/exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically construed as closing the claim to inclusion of materials other than recited ones except ordinary impurities (In re Gray, Ex parte Davis). Nuances: courts have found exceptions where additional items are unrelated to claimed invention (Norian). For Markush/group selections, 'consisting of' signals a closed group; when 'consisting of' appears in a clause of the body it strongly presumes closure of that clause's element, but it limits only that clause (see Multilayer Stretch Cling Film, In re Crish, Mannesmann Demag, and the discussion on interaction with an overall 'comprising' transition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase is between 'consisting of' (closed) and 'comprising' (open). For 102/103 prior art application, absent clear indication in the specification of what the basic/novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' (PPG). Applicant bears the burden of showing additional components/steps would materially change the invention. Can be used to modify method steps; interpret in light of the specification (In re Herz, PPG, AK Steel, In re Janakirama-Rao, Ex parte Hoffman).
